newsitem.title: USA: Security stepped up ahead of Oklahoma bomb trial.
newsitem.headline: Security stepped up ahead of Oklahoma bomb trial.

text.p: Security has been heightened around the federal courthouse in Denver ahead of the start of jury selection on Monday in the Oklahoma City bombing trial.

Security cameras have been installed and concrete blocks assembled around the federal courthouse in downtown Denver, but authorities were tight-lipped about measures implemented to safeguard the hundreds of people involved in the trial.
"We're not going to discuss security. We're ready," Chief Deputy Marshal Larry Homenick said.
Denver Mayor Wellington Webb echoed his sentiments on Thursday, saying a plan was implemented after it was announced on Feb. 20, 1996 that the trial would be moved to Denver.
"Because of the planning I think we're prepared and ready to have the trial. Obviously the best security plan is one that's not announced publicly," he said outside the court.
City officials said the cost of extra police protection for the expected four-month trial would amount to about $500,000, mostly for overtime.

Timothy McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols are charged with the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City that killed 168 people and injured hundreds more in the deadliest attack on civilians in U.S. history.

Prosecutors allege the two carried out the bombing as an act of revenge for the attack on the Branch Davidian sect in Waco, Texas, by federal agents two years earlier. Because of the strong political overtones of the case, security has been strict around the courthouse during pre-trial hearings that have been held since the case was moved here last year.

Lawyers, spectators and journalists have had to go through metal detectors to enter the courtroom. Patrol cars from the Federal Protective Service, which is responsible for federal office buildings, have also been present.

But security measures have been stepped up in the past week. Security cameras were installed at the courthouse and concrete blocks known as jersey barriers were set up around the block that houses the courthouse and the federal office building next door.

Butch Montoya, Denver's deputy mayor and manager of public safety, said no downtown streets would be closed, but the jersey barriers were placed in a parking lane on the street around the courthouse. Entrance to the courthouse will be limited to the front door.

Homenick declined to discuss when McVeigh will be moved to the courthouse from a federal facility in suburban Denver. A living area has been prepared for McVeigh at the courthouse but it was not known if he would be moved back to the federal prison on weekends.
Nichols will be tried separately but no date has been announced.
Some 1,700 journalists have already been accredited to cover the trial and the figure is expected to double by Monday.
